items.stem: Harpreet runs a small factory that needs 9,000 kg of raw material a year. Ordering cost is ₹40 per order and carrying cost is ₹8 per kg per year. Calculate the economic order quantity and the number of orders to be placed in a year.

items.stem: Explain any five uses of financial ratios for an entrepreneur.

(v) Convincing lenders and investors: Good ratios show that the business is sound.

items.stem: Explain any five benefits of intellectual property rights to an entrepreneur.

(v) Attracts investors: Investors value ventures with protected technology or brands.

items.stem: Explain any five uses of break-even analysis for an entrepreneur.
items.answer: (i) Shows the minimum sales needed: The entrepreneur knows the sales required to avoid a loss. (ii) Helps in pricing: The effect of a price change on the BEP can be seen. (iii) Helps in planning profit: Sales needed for a target profit can be found. (iv) Shows the effect of cost changes: A rise in fixed or variable cost raises the BEP. (v) Helps in convincing lenders: A low BEP and a high margin of safety show lower risk.

items.stem: Explain any five myths about entrepreneurship.
items.answer: (i) Entrepreneurs are born, not made: Entrepreneurial skills can be learned through education, training and experience. (ii) Entrepreneurship needs a lot of money: Many ventures start small, and funds can be raised from many sources. (iii) Entrepreneurs are gamblers: They take calculated, moderate risks, not blind gambles. (iv) An entrepreneur must have a new invention: Many succeed by improving existing products or serving new markets. (v) Only young people can be entrepreneurs: People of any age can start ventures. (vi) Entrepreneurship is only for people from business families: First-generation entrepreneurs succeed in many fields.

items.stem:

(i) Which form of organisation would you suggest now, and why? (ii) Which form would suit later when investors join? (iii) State two other factors he should consider.
items.answer: (i) One person company: single owner, limited liability, separate legal entity. (ii) Private company, which can have up to 200 members and issue shares to investors. (iii) Cost and ease of formation; continuity; capital required; nature of business (any two).
items.markingKey: 5 marks: (i) One person company: single owner, limited liability, separate legal entity. (ii) Private company, which can have up to 200 members and issue shares to investors. (iii) Cost and ease of formation; continuity; capital required; nature of business (any two).

items.stem:
Harpreet saw that farmers in his district could not afford tractors. He fitted a motorcycle engine to a small plough, selling it at one-tenth the price of a tractor. He also trains village youths to repair it and reinvests most of his surplus in training more youths.
(i) Identify the frugal features of the product. (ii) Is Harpreet a social entrepreneur? Give two reasons.
items.answer: (i) Low cost; simplicity (only essential features); use of locally available parts; robustness for village use. (ii) Yes: main aim is helping poor farmers and youths; surplus reinvested in the mission; success measured by social impact.
items.markingKey: 5 marks: (i) Low cost; simplicity (only essential features); use of locally available parts; robustness for village use. (ii) Yes: main aim is helping poor farmers and youths; surplus reinvested in the mission; success measured by social impact.

items.stem:
Aarav plans to open a café in Coimbatore, where there are already many cafés, each with its own style, menu and loyal customers. His cousin wants to sell rice in a large wholesale market where hundreds of traders sell the same variety at one price.
(i) Identify the market structure each will face. (ii) What should Aarav do to succeed? (iii) Can the cousin charge a higher price?
items.answer: (i) Aarav: monopolistic competition (many sellers, differentiated products); cousin: perfect competition (many sellers, identical product, uniform price). (ii) Differentiate the café (theme, menu, service) and promote the brand. (iii) No; under perfect competition one price prevails and buyers will go elsewhere.
items.markingKey: 5 marks: (i) Aarav: monopolistic competition (many sellers, differentiated products); cousin: perfect competition (many sellers, identical product, uniform price). (ii) Differentiate the café (theme, menu, service) and promote the brand. (iii) No; under perfect competition one price prevails and buyers will go elsewhere.

items.stem: Diya runs a tuition centre in Agra. In a month she sold 2,650 student-months at ₹2,355 each (unit of sale: one student per month). The month's costs were: materials ₹30,45,750, wages ₹9,46,500, rent and other expenses ₹9,50,000. Calculate the unit cost and the unit margin.

items.stem: Explain any five aims of working capital management.
items.answer: (i) Ensure liquidity: Enough cash is kept to pay bills on time. (ii) Avoid excess current assets: Idle stock and cash earn nothing. (iii) Control debtors: Credit sales are collected on time. (iv) Use supplier credit wisely: Payables are managed to reduce cash needs. (v) Keep optimum inventory: Neither shortage nor excess of stock.

items.stem:
Aryan, a first-generation college graduate in Varanasi, wants to start a small organic-soap business. His parents say that business is only for people from business families, that it needs huge capital and that it is a gamble. Banks have asked for security he does not have.
(i) Identify the myths in the parents' views and correct them. (ii) Identify the obstacle he faces and suggest one way to overcome it.
items.answer: (i) Entrepreneurs come only from business families – first-generation entrepreneurs succeed; needs huge capital – ventures can start small; a gamble – entrepreneurs take calculated risks. (ii) Lack of finance; approach schemes such as MUDRA loans, angel investors, or start small with own savings.
